draft.title: Propaganda and censorship
card: information made to shape what people think and do, often by stirring up emotion. In the First World War, posters and newspaper stories urged men to enlist and people to back the war.
the government controlling what people could read or say. Under the War Precautions Act, officials could stop news from being printed and could read and cut soldiers' letters.
Both had one purpose: to keep up support for the war. One pushed people towards the cause. The other held back information that might weaken their support.
Bad news, such as high casualty numbers, could be kept out of the papers or played down. This meant many people at home did not get a full picture of the fighting.
draft.remember: Propaganda pushed support for the war. Censorship limited information that could weaken it.

a.q: Which of these is an example of censorship?
opts: Officials cut a soldier's letter before it reached home
A poster told men it was their duty to enlist
A newspaper printed a story praising brave soldiers
A speech urged families to buy war bonds
a.why: Censorship means the government controls what people can read or say, such as cutting a letter. The other three try to persuade people to support the war, which is propaganda.
a.clue: Which one stops information instead of persuading?

b.q: A newspaper in Adelaide in 1916 printed only a short note on a battle with very heavy Australian losses. What was the most likely reason?
opts: Censorship aimed to limit news that might reduce support
Propaganda aimed to push more men to enlist
Soldiers had written home to say the battle went well
Newspapers were not allowed to report on any battles
b.why: Censorship let officials keep or play down bad news so support for the war would not fall. Propaganda tries to persuade, but a short note hiding losses limits information. The card does not say newspapers could not report battles at all.
b.clue: Was information being pushed out or held back?

a.best: Officials cut a soldier's letter before it reached home

b.best: Censorship aimed to limit news that might reduce support

check.summary: No problems found. The card is accurate about wartime propaganda and censorship under the War Precautions Act, and both questions have one clearly correct answer that matches the writer's explanations.
